sections.normalized_html: What number is [MATH: 40\%] greater than [MATH: 360]?

A number [MATH: 40\%] greater means applying a new percentage of

[MATH: 100\% + 40\% = 140\%.]

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

[MATH: 140\% = \dfrac{140}{100} = 1.40]

So, to find a number that is [MATH: 40\%] greater than [MATH: 360,] we multiply [MATH: 360] by [MATH: 1.40{:}]

[MATH: 1.40 \cdot 360 = 504]

Therefore, the number that is [MATH: 40\%] greater than [MATH: 360] is [MATH: 504.]

sections.readable_text:
A hospital tracked the number of patient visits in two consecutive years, as shown below.

| Year | Patient visits |
| [MATH: 2020] | [MATH: 30,\!000] |
| [MATH: 2021] | [MATH: 31,\!500] |

The hospital administrator estimated that the percentage increase from [MATH: 2021] to [MATH: 2022] would be four times the percentage increase from [MATH: 2020] to [MATH: 2021.] How many visits did the administrator expect in [MATH: 2022?]

sections.normalized_html:
To find a percentage increase, we use the formula

[MATH: \text{Percentage Increase} = \dfrac{\text{New Value} - \text{Original Value}}{\text{Original Value}} \times 100\%.]

From [MATH: 2020] to [MATH: 2021,] the percentage increase is [MATH: Percentage Increase|= (31, 500 − 30, 000)/(30, 000) × 100%; = (1, 500)/(30, 000) × 100%; = 0.05 × 100%; = 5%.]

Since the percentage increase from [MATH: 2021] to [MATH: 2022] would be four times [MATH: 5\%,] the percentage increase is

[MATH: 4 \times 5 =20\%.]

So, in [MATH: 2021,] the original value is [MATH: 31,\!500] and the percentage increase is [MATH: 20\%.] We use it now to find the new value corresponding to the expected number of visits in [MATH: 2022{:}]

[MATH: 20%|= (New Value − 31, 500)/(31, 500) × 100%; 0.20|= (New Value − 31, 500)/(31, 500); 6, 300|= New Value − 31, 500; New Value|= 37, 800]

Therefore, the administrator expected [MATH: 37,\!800] visits in [MATH: 2022.]
